name: Mencía
say: men-THEE-ah, or as Jaen in Portugal, zhah-EN

lines.s10: Mencía comes from the slate slopes of north west Spain: raspberry, sour cherry and violet, with a stony freshness and fine tannin.
lines.s20: Mencía is the red grape of Bierzo and Ribeira Sacra, in Spain's green north west. It is medium bodied and fragrant, with raspberry, violet and a stony note from slate, fresh rather than heavy.
lines.s45: Mencía grows on the slate of Spain's green north west, in Bierzo and in the canyons of Ribeira Sacra. In the glass it is bright ruby, with raspberry, sour cherry and violet. It feels fresh and stony, medium in body, with fine tannin. Most cellars handle it gently, in steel or older barrels, so the perfume stays in front, and old vines give deeper, firmer wines that keep. Pour it slightly cool with roast pork, octopus or charcuterie. In Ribeira Sacra the vines hang on stone terraces so steep that the grapes come up in baskets or on little rack railways.
lines.sale: Mencía is the red of Bierzo, on the pilgrims' road to Santiago: violet and raspberry with a stony freshness that revives any traveller. A light chill suits it, beside the octopus or the roast pork.

glass.lead: Raspberry, sour cherry and violet over crushed slate, medium bodied and fresh, with fine tannin and a touch of liquorice.

ladder.where: Chantada on the Miño and the Sil's north facing terraces
Amandi's south facing slate, Bierzo's basin and the Dão as Jaen

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium plus, tannin medium and fine, alcohol medium, body medium; old vines on slate add depth and grip.

home.home: The green north west of Spain: Bierzo in León and, in Galicia, Ribeira Sacra, Valdeorras and Monterrei, much of it on slate. Most cellars handle it gently, in steel or used wood, for a fragrant young red; old bush vines on the slopes give deeper, firmer wines with a decade of life.
home.abroad: Across the border it is Jaen, a supple, early ripening partner of Touriga Nacional in the reds of the Dão. Beyond Iberia it is seldom seen.

service.temp: 54 to 59 degrees Fahrenheit, 12 to 15 degrees Celsius; old vine wines a little warmer.
service.glass: A Burgundy bowl, which gathers the violet and raspberry perfume.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary for a young wine; consider it for an old vine bottling after tasting a sample.
service.age: Most within three years; old vine bottlings from slate keep three to ten.

labels.means: The basin in León where Mencía leads the reds, at its deepest from old vines on slate.

guest.a: In weight and freshness, yes: medium bodied, bright and fragrant. It is a little deeper in colour, with liquorice, black pepper and a stony note from slate, so it handles roast pork as well as fish.

guest.q: Is it related to Cabernet Franc?
guest.a: Growers long thought so, since both can smell of raspberry and violet. DNA says no: it is the same grape as Jaen, the red of Portugal's Dão.

guest.q: Should a red really be served this cool?
guest.a: A young Mencía, yes, lightly: a few minutes in the ice bucket lifts the raspberry and the freshness. An old vine bottling wants a little more warmth.

compare.tell: Cabernet Franc is leafier, with green bell pepper and tobacco leaf; Mencía shares the raspberry and violet without the green edge, leaning to sour cherry and pomegranate.
Pinot Noir is paler and silkier, with forest floor; Mencía is deeper in colour, with liquorice, black pepper and a firmer grip.
Gamay is lighter and juicier, often with banana and bubblegum from whole bunch fermentation; Mencía has more colour and tannin, with liquorice and black pepper.

cards.front: Mencía: where is it at home, and on what soil?
cards.back: North west Spain: Bierzo in León, and Ribeira Sacra, Valdeorras and Monterrei in Galicia, its deepest wines from old vines on slate.

cards.front: What is Mencía called in Portugal, and in which region?
cards.back: Jaen, in the Dão, where it is a supple, early ripening partner of Touriga Nacional, Alfrocheiro and Tinta Roriz.

cards.front: Mencía was long linked to Cabernet Franc. What did DNA show?
cards.back: No relation. Profiling showed it to be the same grape as Jaen of Portugal's Dão.

questions.q: A red poured blind is bright ruby and medium bodied, with raspberry, sour cherry, violet and a stony note, fresh acidity and fine tannin. It comes from terraces above a Galician river. Which grape is it?
questions.exp: Raspberry, violet and a stony freshness at medium weight from Ribeira Sacra mark Mencía. Cabernet Franc, the nearest miss, would show a leafy edge of green bell pepper and is no Galician grape.

questions.q: A guest loved a Dão red led by Jaen and asks for the same grape from Spain. Which wine do you bring?
questions.exp: Jaen is Mencía, the red of Bierzo and Ribeira Sacra. Rioja Crianza, the nearest miss, is Tempranillo, which the Dão also grows, under the name Tinta Roriz.

questions.q: A guest wants a light, fresh Spanish red that can take a slight chill beside a plate of octopus. Which bottle fits?
questions.exp: Mencía from Ribeira Sacra is light to medium bodied, fragrant and fresh, and a light chill suits it. Toro and Jumilla are dense, dark and tannic, and Priorat Garnacha is powerful and warm.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it; nothing contradicts TASTE.world old, and the ladder's cool and moderate rungs follow TASTE.clim cool and the Régionale cool to moderate.

Bierzo, Ribeira Sacra, Valdeorras and Monterrei, slate, the gentle cellar, old bush vines with a decade of life, Bierzo's ladder of 2017, botillo and the stone terraces worked by hand with baskets and rack railways all stand on the Codex's own Bierzo and Ribeiro, Ribeira Sacra and Valdeorras records; Jaen in the Dão on the Codex's Dão record and question; the old link to Cabernet Franc on the Régionale trap and on Falstaff and Wein-Plus.

A tale of pilgrims carrying the grape along the road to Santiago as Cabernet Franc appears in trade pages as folklore only and is left out. DNA work suggesting Mencía is a cross of two Portuguese grapes, Alfrocheiro and Patorra, was seen in secondary sources only and is left out.
The floral group carries violet and dried violet: violet is the note every source gives; rose petal and lavender each appeared in one trade page only.

The Codex's GRAPES tell reads Loire texture with Spanish fruit from heroic river slopes and its confuse names pyrazine; both are its own style and no error, but the word pyrazine would be refused in a spoken line here.
